title: A light of the nations (Isaiah 42:6)
hookLine: Israel is called to be "a light of the nations"

lines: A BRUISED REED. A SMOKING WICK.
cards: Chapter forty-two introduces a figure the book calls my servant, and before it says the word light, it shows what this servant won't do.

"He shall not cry, nor lift up, nor cause his voice to be heard in the street. A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench". No shouting. No snapping what's already cracked.
No blowing out a flame that's nearly gone. Then, a few lines later, comes the calling.

teach.h: NO SHOUTING, NO BREAKING THE REED.
teach.b: Here it is, in verse six: "I the LORD have called thee in righteousness, and will hold thine hand." And then: I will give thee for a covenant of the people, for a light of the nations.
The King James says Gentiles; the Hebrew word, goyim, means nations, and that's how the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation renders it. So who is the servant?
Jewish tradition hears the people Israel in these chapters, and the servant comes back in a few days. Today, stay with the light. It doesn't shout.
It doesn't break the bruised reed or snuff out the smoking wick. This is not a searchlight sweeping the streets. It's closer to a lamp in a window: simply there, and people find their way by it.

The next verse says what the light is for: "To open the blind eyes, to bring out the prisoners from the prison." Light, in Isaiah, is something that frees people. Jewish writers have taken this calling in different ways.
Some hear a call to live by the Torah so faithfully that others notice. Some hear a call to justice, opening eyes and prison doors.
Some hear mainly a promise held by God: I will hold thine hand.
What they share is that the light is a calling, not a trophy.
A lamp doesn't light itself to be admired.

how: Isaiah 42 is read in synagogue as a haftarah, and the phrase a light to the nations is used in Jewish teaching for the calling of the people Israel, understood in different ways by different communities.

games.q: what does “a light of the nations” mean?
o: a calling to shine quietly so others find their way
a promise that Israel will rule over other peoples
a lamp kept burning in the Temple day and night

games.q: a light of the nations — tap the pairs.

s: the servant in Isaiah 42 shouts in the streets
he shall not cry, nor cause his voice to be heard in the street.

games.q: you're called to be a light. you meet someone cracked like a bruised reed. what does Isaiah's servant do?
o: correct them loudly so they learn.
walk past to find someone stronger.
games.why: "a bruised reed shall he not break." the light Isaiah describes is quiet and careful with what's already cracked.

practice: Let one person come to mind who is a bit of a bruised reed right now, cracked but not broken, or a wick burning low.

Ask the quiet question, not the loud one: what small thing would help them see their way, a word of credit, a door held open, an answer to the message they sent? If you pray, you can hold the verse: I will hold thine hand.
